title: Headache
summary: Headaches have many possible triggers. This overview cannot identify the cause of an individual headache.
possibleCauses: Common causes listed by the NHS include a cold or flu, stress, dehydration, missed meals, eyesight problems, posture, and alcohol.
associatedSymptoms: A headache may occur with cold or flu symptoms. Sudden severe pain, weakness, speech or balance problems, confusion, vision loss, or a stiff neck need urgent attention.
selfCare: Drink water, rest, try to relax, and avoid skipping meals. Check the product label and ask a pharmacist or doctor before using any medicine.
warningSigns: A sudden extremely painful headache, seizure, weakness or numbness, difficulty speaking or walking, confusion, vision loss, stiff neck with high temperature, or a non-fading rash.
whenToSeeDoctor: Seek medical advice if it is worsening, not improving, recurring, or accompanied by concerning symptoms. Sudden severe symptoms require emergency help.

title: Fever
summary: For adults, the NHS describes a high temperature as usually 38°C or above. A fever is often a symptom of infection; this page is adult information, not guidance for babies or children.
possibleCauses: Many causes are possible; the NHS says a high temperature is often caused by the body fighting an infection such as a cold or flu.
associatedSymptoms: Feeling hot or cold, shivering, sweating, or warm and red skin can occur. A thermometer reading below 38°C does not always rule out feeling feverish.
selfCare: Rest and drink fluids. Follow the product label and ask a pharmacist or doctor before taking medicine, especially for children, pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, or chronic conditions.
warningSigns: Severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, loss of consciousness, or sudden severe worsening needs emergency attention.
whenToSeeDoctor: Contact a clinician or pharmacist if a fever treated at home is not improving or is getting worse. Seek earlier advice for a child, pregnancy, older age, or chronic illness.

title: Cough
summary: A cough has different possible causes and MedLens cannot determine which one applies to you.
possibleCauses: Respiratory infections are one possible context. A clinician can assess other causes.
associatedSymptoms: A respiratory infection can also involve sneezing, a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, headache, muscle aches, fever, or feeling unwell.
selfCare: Rest and drink fluids. A pharmacist can advise about symptom relief. Do not use medicine based on this app; check the label and consult a pharmacist or doctor.
warningSigns: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, coughing blood, or a cough that quickly becomes severe needs urgent medical advice. Severe breathing difficulty is an emergency.
whenToSeeDoctor: The NHS advises medical advice for a cough lasting more than 3 weeks, a very bad or rapidly worsening cough, feeling very unwell, chest pain, breathing difficulty, or blood in sputum.
sourceName: NHS: Cough; NHS: Respiratory tract infections

title: Common cold
summary: Cold-like symptoms overlap with flu, COVID-19, and other illnesses. Symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish them.
possibleCauses: The NHS describes the common cold as a viral infection that spreads easily.
associatedSymptoms: Symptoms can include blocked or runny nose, sneezing, sore throat, hoarse voice, cough, tiredness, high temperature, aching muscles, or pressure in the ears and face.
selfCare: Rest, drink fluids, and avoid smoke. For advice about any medicine, check its label and ask a pharmacist or doctor; products may not suit children, pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, or chronic conditions.
warningSigns: Shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, very high temperature, or severe rapid worsening.
whenToSeeDoctor: Ask a clinician if symptoms worsen, a high temperature lasts more than 3 days, symptoms have not improved after 10 days, cough lasts more than 3 weeks, or you have a long-term condition or weakened immune system.

title: Sore throat
summary: Sore throats are common and often improve on their own, but some symptoms need prompt or emergency care.
possibleCauses: The NHS says sore throats are usually caused by viruses such as cold or flu, or smoking; less commonly, bacteria or other throat conditions can be involved.
associatedSymptoms: Pain on swallowing, dry or scratchy throat, redness, bad breath, mild cough, or swollen neck glands may occur.
selfCare: Drink water, rest, choose cool or soft foods, and avoid smoky places. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for personal advice; do not use app content to choose a medicine.
warningSigns: Difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling because swallowing is not possible, a high-pitched breathing sound, or severe symptoms getting worse quickly.
whenToSeeDoctor: Seek medical advice for a very high temperature, dehydration signs, weakened immune system, worsening symptoms, or symptoms that concern you.

title: Acidity / heartburn
summary: A burning feeling in the chest can have different causes. Crushing chest pain can be an emergency and should not be assumed to be heartburn.
possibleCauses: The NHS notes stomach acid irritating the stomach lining or throat as a common cause of indigestion; some foods, smoking, pregnancy, stress, and some medicines can contribute.
associatedSymptoms: Heartburn may feel like burning in the chest, often after eating. Indigestion can also include fullness, bloating, nausea, or burping.
selfCare: Notice and avoid personal food or drink triggers. Avoid lying down soon after a meal. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice, particularly during pregnancy or when taking other medicines.
warningSigns: Crushing chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, fainting, or sudden severe symptoms need emergency attention.
whenToSeeDoctor: Seek medical advice for recurrent or severe symptoms, difficulty swallowing, repeated vomiting, unexplained weight loss, blood in vomit or stool, or symptoms that persist.

title: Indigestion
summary: Indigestion can cause upper abdominal discomfort, but symptoms such as severe pain or bleeding may indicate another problem.
possibleCauses: The NHS lists stomach acid irritation as a common cause. Food and drink, smoking, stress, pregnancy, some medicines, and other digestive conditions may contribute.
associatedSymptoms: Heartburn, fullness or bloating, nausea, burping, or bringing food or bitter fluid into the mouth can occur.
selfCare: Avoid foods or drinks that seem to trigger symptoms and avoid eating close to bedtime. Ask a pharmacist or doctor before using a medicine, especially if pregnant or managing a chronic condition.
warningSigns: Severe chest pain, difficulty breathing, blood in vomit or stool, or sudden severe pain needs urgent medical attention.
whenToSeeDoctor: Seek advice if symptoms recur, are severe, persist, or come with difficulty swallowing, repeated vomiting, unexplained weight loss, or blood.

title: Sneezing
summary: Sneezing can occur with a cold or an allergy. This information cannot determine which is the cause.
possibleCauses: The NHS lists viral colds and allergic rhinitis (for example, reactions to pollen, dust mites, mould, or animal dander) among possible explanations.
associatedSymptoms: A cold may include a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, cough, and tiredness. Allergic rhinitis may include itchy or watery eyes and an itchy nose.
selfCare: For possible pollen exposure, the NHS suggests showering and changing clothes after being outdoors and keeping windows closed when pollen is high. A pharmacist can advise about ongoing symptoms.
warningSigns: Sudden swelling of the mouth, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, fainting, or rapidly worsening symptoms can signal a serious emergency.
whenToSeeDoctor: Seek advice if symptoms are worsening, not improving, or interfering with daily life. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for guidance before treatment.
sourceName: NHS: Common cold; NHS: Allergic rhinitis

title: Muscle pain
summary: Muscle pain can be related to activity or a wider health problem; this overview cannot identify the cause.
possibleCauses: MedlinePlus lists tension, overuse, injury, stress, some infections, and other medical conditions as possible causes.
associatedSymptoms: It may affect one or several muscles. Fever, weakness, swelling, redness, or difficulty moving can be important associated symptoms.
selfCare: For mild pain after activity, rest the affected area and avoid further strain. Ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure or have another condition or take medicines.
warningSigns: Difficulty breathing or swallowing, inability to move a body part, severe weakness, high fever with a very stiff neck, or sudden severe symptoms require urgent or emergency care.
whenToSeeDoctor: Contact a clinician if pain lasts more than 3 days, is severe or unexplained, there is redness or swelling, or it followed a medicine change.

title: Fatigue
summary: Feeling tired sometimes is common. Persistent fatigue with no clear reason may need professional assessment.
possibleCauses: The NHS lists lack of sleep, lifestyle factors, stress, depression, hormonal changes, some illnesses, treatments, and medicines among possible causes.
associatedSymptoms: Notice whether tiredness occurs with weight change, mood changes, palpitations, breathlessness, unusual thirst, or sleep-related breathing symptoms.
selfCare: Try regular sleep and a relaxing bedtime routine. Do not self-diagnose; ask a clinician if fatigue is persistent or affecting daily activities.
warningSigns: Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or sudden severe worsening needs emergency attention.
whenToSeeDoctor: The NHS advises seeing a GP if tiredness lasts for weeks without explanation, affects daily life, or comes with other concerning symptoms.
